source.title: Where Do Large Learning Rates Lead Us?
source.authors: Ildus Sadrtdinov; M. Kodryan; Eduard Pokonechny; E. Lobacheva; D. Vetrov

record.tranche_reason: Tests how initial learning-rate regimes affect held-out performance and a proposed correlate of generalization using controlled pre-training, fine-tuning, and weight averaging; these differ from the listed versions' interventions and measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests initial learning-rate regimes, fine-tuning, and weight averaging. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected architecture, optimizer comparisons, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Cited results from prior work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study tests initial learning rates and subsequent schedules, which none of V1–V8 names. Its sharpness analysis uses mean stochastic gradient norm, not V7's magnitude-aware weight perturbations. Adam and SGD are used in different architecture settings without a controlled optimizer comparison. No listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that moderately large initial learning rates just above the convergence threshold provide the best starting points for fine-tuning or weight averaging in their tested settings, locate basins of well-generalizing solutions, and coincide with sparse learning of useful features. Larger initial rates can recover quality with a gradual schedule. Their separate gradient-norm sharpness analysis finds no consistent relationship across different pre-trained starting points, despite positive trends within a shared starting point.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies initial learning-rate regimes and subsequent fine-tuning or weight averaging; it does not use the original versions' random-label, width, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with initial learning-rate regime, fine-tuning rate, schedule, architecture, dataset, and controlled versus practical setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Initial learning rates just above the convergence threshold give the best subsequent fine-tuning or averaging results in the main setting. Higher initial rates degrade results with a single drop; an intermediate stage through subregime 2A largely restores accuracy. Effects are weaker for ConvNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial learning-rate selection and the subsequent schedule jointly affect held-out performance; moderately high initial rates can outperform small fixed rates in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed training-loss level, mean stochastic gradient norm and test error show a positive trend within fine-tuning runs sharing a pre-trained checkpoint, but this relationship can break or reverse across different pre-trained checkpoints. Similar test errors can accompany almost twofold differences in this sharpness measure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mean stochastic gradient norm does not consistently rank generalization across the tested pretraining histories.

record.problems: The study is empirical and limited to specified image and synthetic datasets and architectures. The authors note that findings may not generalize to other settings. Some comparisons are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The sharpness analysis uses mean stochastic gradient norm and reports no direct correlation across fine-tuning runs from different pre-trained points.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results left out. Figure-only numerical values were not reconstructed. Prior-work results cited in the introduction and related work were excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting capacity and the natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Controlled adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparisons and the effects of tuning or switching optimizers.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipes that compensate for large batches.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance, its ranking of generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Influence-based identification and removal of memorized training examples, with random-removal controls and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row links to none are retained. Their states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, without disputing the reported learning-rate effects. The citation to Feldman and Zhang motivates future work rather than testing V8. No omitted result in the supplied text warrants a verdict on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness. The study measures mean stochastic gradient norm sharpness instead.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Pre-train at first-regime PLRs, then fine-tune at first-regime FLRs; compare test accuracy with pre-training and training from scratch.
rows.value: Fine-tuning with FLR ≤ PLR does not noticeably change pre-trained accuracy; FLR > PLR can significantly improve it, but does not provide a considerably better solution than training from scratch with the same FLR.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison stated in the Results text; no numerical accuracies are given there.
rows.check: The learning-rate comparison fits no version; partial is not a state for any listed claim.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.stage_stated: pre-training followed by fine-tuning or SWA
rows.operation_detail: Pre-train in subregime 2A, then fine-tune with first-regime FLRs or use SWA.
rows.value: Subregime 2A gives significantly better fine-tuning and SWA results than regime 1; fine-tuning with any FLR yields minima of the same quality.
rows.note: Qualitative outcome stated in the Results text.
rows.check: Improvement from initial learning-rate selection fits no version.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.stage_stated: pre-training followed by fine-tuning or SWA
rows.operation_detail: Pre-train in subregime 2B, then fine-tune with first-regime FLRs or use SWA.
rows.value: Both SWA and fine-tuning quality degrades; fine-tuned solutions begin to differ in test accuracy across FLRs.
rows.note: The authors describe deterioration relative to 2A and growing differences across fine-tuning rates.
rows.check: Deterioration relative to subregime 2A does not reverse any listed version.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Pre-train in subregime 2B, then reduce the learning rate through subregime 2A before fine-tuning at a first-regime FLR.
rows.baseline: Fine-tuning directly from 2B to the given FLR; fine-tuning after pre-training in 2A
rows.value: Gradual fine-tuning through lower second-regime LRs restores quality, reaching almost the same test accuracy as usual fine-tuning after pre-training in 2A.
rows.note: The text describes the comparisons but does not give numerical accuracy values.
rows.check: Schedule recovery fits no version. The recovery uses an additional 200-epoch intermediate stage, followed by 200 epochs at the final learning rate.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Pre-train in regime 3, then fine-tune with small first-regime FLRs.
rows.baseline: Training from scratch with the same FLRs
rows.value: Fine-tuning after regime 3 can be beneficial compared with training from scratch with the same small FLRs.
rows.note: The authors state the qualitative comparison and conjecture an optimization explanation.
rows.check: The benefit of regime-3 initialization fits no version; partial has no claim-relative interpretation.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune practical ResNet-18 models after pre-training at different PLRs.

conditions.value: practical, with augmentation and weight decay

rows.value: At the best points of subregime 2A, fine-tuning reaches test accuracy of ∼ 95%, no worse than that of a standard LR schedule.
rows.note: The text reports this accuracy and comparison explicitly.
rows.check: Subject should be practical ResNet-18, without the sphere constraint, rather than SI ResNet-18. Approximately 95% accuracy is the study's result, but the standard-schedule comparison cites reference [49], rather than a matched baseline reported here. No listed version is measured.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Measure adopted sharpness as mean stochastic gradient norm and compare it with test error at fixed training loss.

conditions.value: fine-tuning solutions from different pre-trained points

rows.value: The authors report no direct correlation across fine-tuning runs from different pre-trained points; solutions with similar test error can have sharpness values differing on average by almost a factor of two.
rows.note: This is a different sharpness measure from V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure. The comparison is reported at a fixed training loss.
rows.check: Mean stochastic gradient norm cannot establish V7's magnitude-aware perturbation effect. The reported cross-pretraining failure is accurate for this different measure; within runs sharing a pre-trained checkpoint, the authors report a positive sharpness–test-error trend. Values at the fixed training loss are interpolated between adjacent checkpoints.

rows.subject: SI ConvNet
rows.stage_stated: pre-training followed by fine-tuning or SWA
rows.operation_detail: Pre-train at different PLRs, then fine-tune or use SWA.
rows.value: The second-regime effects are less pronounced: fine-tuning and SWA improve less in 2A, and the detrimental effect of 2B on fine-tuning is almost leveled out.
rows.note: The text reports the architecture-specific qualification; numerical values are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Both architectures being compared are convolutional, so this is not V3. The architecture-dependent learning-rate effects fit no listed version.

rows.subject: SI ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Train to convergence from scratch with fixed PLRs near the boundary between regimes 1 and 2 and compare with fine-tuned results.
rows.measure: test accuracy and epochs to convergence
rows.value: Converged minima have approximately the same test accuracy as fine-tuned solutions at corresponding PLRs, but require immensely more epochs to reach.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that the best fine-tuning accuracy at PLR ≈ 10−3 is unattainable within any realistic epoch budget.
rows.check: The measured models are trained from scratch at fixed learning rates until loss reaches 10^-3, with a maximum of 20,000 epochs; fine-tuned models are the comparison. This is not a width sweep or batch-size comparison.

rows.subject: Practical ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune after pre-training at different PLRs in the practical setting.

conditions.value: SGD with momentum, weight decay, and data augmentation

rows.value: Fine-tuning in 2A converges to similar optima regardless of FLR; at larger PLRs, fine-tuning leads to diverse minima.
rows.note: Qualitative outcomes are stated in the text; the figure provides plotted results.
rows.check: The practical learning-rate and solution-similarity comparison fits no version.
